title: Always there
hookLine: women's stories were often unrecorded, but they were always there

lines: THE RECORD OFTEN RAN THE OTHER WAY.
cards: Open the book of Exodus to its first chapter. A king of Egypt orders that every Hebrew baby boy be killed at birth. The text never gives that king's name.
He is just Pharaoh. But two women stand between his order and the babies, and the text names them both: Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives.
The man with the throne goes unnamed; two women who deliver babies get their names written down. For long stretches of the history we've been walking through, it ran the other way.

teach.b: "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." A quiet refusal in a birthing room, by women with no army.
Later books name more women: Miriam with her timbrel at the sea, Deborah judging Israel under a palm tree, Ruth on the road, Esther in the palace.
Then come the long centuries after the Bible. Much of what was written down in them was written by men, about what men argued over in the study house and the court.
A great deal of women's lives went unrecorded. Who lit the candles each Friday in a cold room. Who ran the shop while her husband studied.
Who kept the recipes, songs and accounts, and taught a child the first blessing.

But the record leaves traces: in the margins of old books, in letters, in the memoir a merchant woman named Glikl wrote in Yiddish for her children, in Yiddish prayers written for women to say over the candles and the dough.
Historians have spent a long time gathering them. So today's line isn't a complaint or a slogan. It's a correction to how we read.
When a page of history seems to be all men, it often means the women were in the next room, keeping the whole thing alive, and nobody was taking notes.
Over the next days you'll meet some of them by name: a seamstress who started a school, a rabbi, a girl at a lectern, a writer, a teacher.

how: Jewish communities and schools increasingly teach women's history alongside the familiar story, reading the women of the Bible closely and gathering the letters, memoirs and Yiddish prayers that women left behind.

o: a promise that God never leaves a person on their own
a name for the synagogue's ever-burning lamp
women present through Jewish history, often unrecorded

p: the midwives who saved the babies
the king the text leaves unnamed

s: in Exodus, the king of Egypt is named but the midwives are not
it's the other way around. the text names Shiphrah and Puah and calls the king only Pharaoh.
the midwives refused the king's order
"the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them."
women left no traces in the written record after the Bible
they left letters, a memoir like Glikl's, and Yiddish prayers written for women.

games.q: you're a Hebrew midwife in Egypt. the king has ordered you to kill every baby boy you deliver. what do you do?
o: obey, because he is the king.
quietly refuse, and let the babies live.
run away and leave the women alone.
games.why: they refused: "the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." and the text writes down their names.

practice: Call up a woman from your own family line, or someone else's: a grandmother, a great-aunt, a neighbor who raised half the street. What do you actually know: her name, where she lived, one thing she made or said or kept?
Notice where your knowledge stops, the edge where her story went unrecorded, and rest with her there, just as she was.

wordCard.voice: Always there. The women of Jewish history, from the midwives of Exodus to the grandmothers no one wrote about, present the whole time, even where the record left them out. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: nobody was taking notes. The women were there all along. See you tomorrow.
